rv.q: “It’s the first full-scale play that Guare has written in some time...Not to worry, though: ‘Nantucket Sleigh Ride’ is as good as anything he’s given us.
Better to just sit back and enjoy the crazy ride.
Or sometimes the audience does.

But by the time Guare gets to the giant lobster (don't ask) he seems to have run out of imagination — or the inclination to round up his disjointed memories and wrestle them into a coherent plot with some kind of thematic backbone.
It's too bad, then, that the efforts of the hard-working performers and other creatives have been put in service of a trivial play that doesn't deserve them.
If you allow the plot to unravel of its own accord, you'll find that the ride is fast and fun and tenderhearted without triggering any sort of mental whiplash.
It’s a mostly comic tale of ambition, neglect, corruption and deception that has far too many twists and teases and tumult to hazard even a brief outline.

The last scenes, however, descend into a feebler and flatter conclusion than the rip-roaring romp with a surfeit of funny characters, stellar performances, and witty turns of phrase that came before them.
If the parts don't appear to amount to anything substantial, well, this one's more about the ride than the destination.
"There are moments in this zany comedy that merit applause but the work on the whole is unfulfilled and lacks a clear-cut focus.

A fitfully entertaining two-act caper, the essential and disappointing problem with Nantucket Sleigh Ride is that its antic story does not rise to a higher power: There is no significance to it, no raison d’être, no message to take away afterwards to mull over.
You may wonder—like my seat neighbor—what the point of all it was (even when a lobster is electrocuted in one standout scene).
The play initially has a fascinating premise but goes off the deep end in its second half.

Larroquette is a magnificent narrator...While attempting to follow the first act’s ever-twisting plot, however, one’s mind may drift to incidental problems with the play and its production. For starters, Jerry Zaks’ direction emphasizes the farcical situations, but most of the eye-popping performances are merely manic and not remotely amusing.

Nantucket Sleigh Ride is really a kind of carryall containing a load of stray plot devices -- including some remarkably tasteless jokes -- that Guare has strenuously, but unsuccessfully, attempted to arrange into a coherent and amusing pattern.
Sadly, I jumped ship before the whale wore itself out.

“Zaks knows just how to build comedy without forcing it; keeping the energy flowing without rushing his actors or letting them fall...Not one cue is dropped; not one comedic moment left unexploited...’Nantucket Sleigh Ride’ is a whale of a show.
The whole affair is strange, funny, and somewhat confounding—a farcical period-piece poking at questions of artistic ambition and inspiration, the process of writing, and the shaping of memory.
There’s both whimsy and wisdom in “Nantucket Sleigh Ride,” making this unusual work more than just another day at the beach.
A farce, a puzzle and a jumble of pop culture references with a lot of laughs, and it may leave you feeling unglued.
I just found this play too convoluted to grasp its symbolism.
For all its smarts and high spirits, 'Nantucket Sleigh Ride' isn't so much a whale of a tale. It's one that got away.
The utmost effort of the cast and creative team cannot overcome the pitch and roll of this tumultuous ride that never dives beneath the surface to discover the meaning of the contrived story.
A polished production but it carries too much absurdist blubber to make its pursuit more than momentarily worthwhile.

cn.t: Guare's absurdist farce divides critics with its manic, surreal storytelling and pop culture chaos. Larroquette earns praise, but many find the play incomprehensible and overlong, while others embrace its zany energy and dark humor.
